opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the reason I see it as a milestone is that it closes a loop that has never been closed before.

Right now, every robot in the world is ultimately bottlenecked by human labor. Humans design them, humans machine the parts, humans assemble them, humans debug them when something goes wrong. So no matter how capable an individual robot becomes, the total number of robots, and how fast that number grows, is still capped by how many skilled people we have and how fast they can work. It's a linear process.

The moment robots can build robots, including assembling parts, doing the fiddly wiring, testing and fixing each other, that constraint goes away. Growth becomes multiplicative instead of additive, almost like biological reproduction. One robot helps make two, two help make four. That's a phase change, not just an incremental improvement.

There's also a technical reason I care about it. Manufacturing a robot is one of the hardest manipulation tasks you can pick. It involves tiny connectors, cables, screws, delicate alignment, and lots of variation. If a robot can reliably do that, it's a strong signal that it has the dexterity and generality to do most physical work humans do. So it's a good benchmark as well as an economic turning point.

And the last piece is data. Robot learning is starved for real-world data. If robots can produce more robots cheaply, you get more machines out in the world collecting experience, which makes the models better, which makes the robots better at building robots. That flywheel is what I think really unlocks the field. So to me, self-replication, in this practical, factory-floor sense, is the point where robotics stops being a craft and starts scaling like software.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly compares robots making more robots to biological reproduction and describes this as practical self-replication.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it the way you'd think about any technology that turns a corner from being a tool into being a system that sustains itself.

Right now, every robot in the world is built by human hands, or by machines that humans set up and babysit. That puts a hard ceiling on how many robots can exist. The bottleneck isn't demand, and honestly it's not even the algorithms anymore. The bottleneck is assembly: tightening screws, routing cables, calibrating joints, running quality checks. Those are exactly the kinds of dexterous, repetitive, slightly variable tasks that humans are good at and that we've struggled to automate.

So when a robot can assemble another robot, two things happen at once. First, you've solved a very hard general-purpose manipulation problem, because building a robot is not a single task, it's hundreds of small tasks with tolerances and fine motor control. If a robot can do that, it can do a lot of other things in a factory or a home. It's a proof of capability.

Second, and this is the part that I think people underestimate, the cost curve changes shape. Today, if you want ten times as many robots, you need something close to ten times as many workers on the assembly line. Once robots build robots, each unit you produce also increases your production capacity. That's a compounding loop. It's the same dynamic that made semiconductors cheap, where the machines that make chips got better because of the chips they made.

I'm not saying it's self-replication in some science-fiction sense. There's still a supply chain, there are still humans designing, deciding, and supervising. But the moment the physical labor of making robots is itself done by robots, the industry stops being limited by human hands. That's the milestone. Everything before it is a prototype era. Everything after it is a scaling era.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots building other robots and each new unit increasing production capacity in a compounding loop, conveying robot production as a form of reproduction. Its caveat rejects science-fiction-style self-replication, not this more limited idea.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a milestone because it changes how much robot development depends on us. Today, even if a robot can work autonomously, people still have to manufacture it, assemble it, and maintain it. If robots can build other robots, they can begin to take on that whole process.

That could let us scale robotic systems much faster, especially in places where it’s difficult or dangerous for people to work. But I’d distinguish assembling a copy from actually improving the design. Building themselves would be a major step toward independence; it wouldn’t automatically mean they could invent better versions of themselves.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots building other robots and calls this “assembling a copy,” communicating self-building as a form of reproduction.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a milestone because it changes the relationship between robots and human labor. Today, even a very capable robot depends on people to build it, assemble it, and maintain the production system behind it. If robots can build other robots, that dependence starts to shift.

The important part isn’t simply a robot putting parts together. It’s whether robots can handle the whole process reliably—recognizing mistakes, checking quality, and adapting when something doesn’t fit. That would demonstrate a much broader capability than performing one repetitive task.

It could also make robot production easier to scale. But I would distinguish building themselves from designing themselves: a robot assembling another robot from a human-designed plan is already a significant achievement, without implying that it can independently invent its next generation.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes robots building other robots and says this shifts their dependence on human labor, framing robot construction as robots producing more robots.
